tasks.title: Say what kind of redirect a status is
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/redirects.js`, make `redirectKind(status)` take a status number. For the five redirects, `301`, `302`, `303`, `307` and `308`, it gives back `{ permanent, keepsPost }`:

- `permanent`: `true` when the move is for good, `false` when it is for now
- `keepsPost`: `true` when a `POST` arrives at the new address still a `POST`, with its body, and `false` when it is turned into a `GET`

For any other status it gives back `null`.

Check calls `redirectKind` with each of the five redirects and with statuses that are not redirects.
nextSteps: Start with the statuses that are not one of the five.
Find in the lesson which redirects are for good.
Find which ones send a POST on as it was.
Run `node run.js` and read the three Task 1 lines.
hints: Two questions per redirect, each answered with true or false. The lesson's list of five answers both.
Only 301 and 308 are for good. Only 307 and 308 promise to send the request again as it was; 301, 302 and 303 end up as a GET.
Keep an object keyed by status, like `{ 301: { permanent: true, keepsPost: false }, ... }`, and `return kinds[status] ?? null`.

tasks.title: See where an address leads, without going there
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `whereTo(address)` send **one** request for `address` without following a redirect. When the answer is a redirect, a status from 300 to 399 with a `location` header, it gives back the whole address that `location` points to, as text, read against `address`. Otherwise it gives back `null`.

Check starts a server of its own that answers with redirects whose `location` is a path, a whole address and a path without a slash at the start, and with answers that are not redirects. It counts the requests its server received.
nextSteps: Tell `fetch` not to follow redirects, with the option the lesson shows.
Read the status and the `location` header of the answer.
Give back `null` unless it is a redirect.
Turn the location into a whole address, read against `address`, and run `node run.js`.
hints: Without being told, `fetch` follows a redirect and hands you the answer from the new address. Your server then receives two requests, and the redirect is gone.
`{ redirect: 'manual' }` in the options keeps the redirect answer. `new URL(location, address)` reads a location against the address you asked for, whatever form it has.
`const response = await fetch(address, { redirect: 'manual' })`, return `null` when the status is outside 300 to 399 or `location` is `null`, and otherwise `return new URL(location, address).href`.

tasks.title: Follow an address step by step
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `trail(address, most)` follow the redirects from `address` one at a time, and give back the list of every whole address it asked for, in order: `address` first, and last the one whose answer is not a redirect. When the answer is still a redirect after `most` redirects, it throws an `Error` instead, without asking any further.

Check starts a server of its own with trails of redirects of different lengths and a loop, and counts the requests its server received.
nextSteps: Keep a list that starts with `address`.
Ask where each address leads; your function from Task 2 can do that.
Add each new address to the list until one leads nowhere.
Before you follow a redirect, check whether `most` redirects are already used up, then run `node run.js`.
hints: A loop that follows redirects needs two ways out, as asking again did: an answer that is not a redirect, and a limit.
`whereTo` gives back the next address, or `null` at the end of the trail. The list has one more address than the redirects it followed.
`let next = await whereTo(address)`, then `while (next !== null) { if (asked.length > most) throw new Error('Too many redirects'); asked.push(next); next = await whereTo(next) }`, and `return asked`.
